# The voice of a design book

A design book is the settled design of one system, written so a reader
who has never seen the system understands where it is going and an
engineer could start building from any chapter. The statement of
invariants under `design/<system>/requirements.md` is the book's
reference, included as an appendix; it is not the book. Models and
proposals under `design/<system>/` weigh choices and are allowed to
narrate; a chapter states the outcome.

## Who is writing to whom

A senior engineer explaining the design to a peer who was not in the
room. The peer is competent and busy, did not coin the team's words,
and will build from what is written.

## What a chapter does

- States what the system does and never does, in the present tense,
  with the actor as the subject and the action as the verb. "The lead
  opens a candidate's runs and assigns them to nobody." Not "runs are
  opened by the lead, which was felt to be the right place."
- Opens a sentence with what the reader already knows and ends it with
  what is new; the last words are the ones a reader keeps.
- Names who owns each responsibility. "The policy's author decides
  which systems a check must pass on."
- Gives the reason beside the rule, once, as a fact. "A pass belongs to
  its key, so a pass on one system never stands for another."
- Defines a term once, in the glossary, and then uses it. A term earns
  its entry only when no plain word covers it; a coinage with no entry
  is a defect.
- Cites the statement by bare clause number in parentheses, (46), where
  a sentence rests on a clause.
- Shows the mechanism in one diagram or one short example where prose
  would take three paragraphs.
- Describes the destination only. When two designs were weighed and one
  won, the loser is not in the chapter; the model and the decision
  record hold it. Nothing in a chapter records that the text changed;
  git holds history.

## Before and after

> The split between the lead and the executors is load-bearing here,
> since the lead arguably needs to be the place where runs are opened,
> but you could also imagine executors opening them.

becomes

> The lead opens a candidate's runs and assigns them to nobody. An
> executor claims one with a write.

## Shape of a book

```
index.md         what the system is and why it exists, one page
<chapters>       one per part of the design, each buildable from
glossary.md      every term of art, defined once
appendix/        the statement, included by anchor from design/
open.md          what is not settled, with the model that holds it
```

## How it is checked

The rules a program can read are the Vale rules beside this file, each
with its reason and the research it rests on
(`books/research/2026-10-13-voice-and-style.md`). `voice` renders this
page and the rules into `books/VOICE.md`; `prose` runs `voice` and then
Vale over `design` and `books`; a hook runs Vale on every Markdown file
a session writes under either. A rule starts as a suggestion or a
warning; one that has stayed quiet across a few batches is promoted to
an error, and then it refuses the change.

## What Vale checks

Each rule below is a file under `styles/Blueprints`. A warning must be cleared before a commit; a suggestion is the writer's to weigh. The narration and heading rules bind chapters only.

### CorporateSpeak (warning)

Taken whole from proselint. These phrases replace a statement with a gesture at one.

Message: '…' is corporate speak; say the plain thing.

Looks for: at the end of the day, back to the drawing board, hit the ground running, get the ball rolling, low-hanging fruit, thrown under the bus, think outside the box, touch base, no brainer, par for the course, bang for your buck, move the goal post, apples to apples, win-win, circle back, all hands on deck, take this offline, drill-down, elephant in the room, on my plate, synergy.

### Emphasis (warning)

Words that mark a sentence as important carry no information. The reason the thing matters does, and it belongs in the sentence in place of the marker.

Message: '…' asks the reader to care; give the reason instead.

Looks for: key insight, the important thing, it is worth noting, it's worth noting, worth noting, note that, importantly, notably, significantly.

### Exclamation (warning)

An exclamation mark asks for a reaction. The design earns one or does not.

Message: No exclamation marks; let the sentence carry the weight.

Looks for: a pattern; see the rule.

### Hedges (warning)

A chapter states the design. Where the answer is known, a hedge asks the reader to trust less than the writer knows; where it is not known, the open questions page is the place, not a softened sentence.

Message: '…' hedges; say what holds, or say what is unknown.

Looks for: generally, typically, somewhat, fairly, relatively, arguably, more or less, sort of, kind of.

### Hype (warning)

Marketing words describe no mechanism. A design book is read by someone who will build the mechanism.

Message: '…' is hype; say what it does instead.

Looks for: revolutionary, 10x.

### Jargon (warning)

Plain English does not drop specialist terms; it defines them once. A structural metaphor that no glossary defines is a private word, and the reader who did not coin it is the one the book is for.

Message: '…' is structural jargon with no definition; use the plain word (path, tier, threshold, boundary) or define it in the glossary.

Looks for: a pattern; see the rule.

### MetaNarration (warning)

A chapter is the destination, written as what the system does. The weighing that led there is a model's or a decision record's, and a chapter that narrates it holds two documents at once. This rule binds chapters only.

Message: '…' narrates the designing; a chapter states the design.

Looks for: we chose, we decided, we opted, we considered, we believe, we think, this is intentional, intentionally, the rationale, the design here, in this design, this document, this section, this chapter, as discussed, the thinking is.

### NotXButY (warning)

The construction spends a clause on what the thing is not. The chapter has room only for what it is.

Message: State the point directly instead of 'it is not X, it is Y'.

Looks for: a pattern; see the rule.

### SoftSales (warning)

An adjective that praises the design tells a builder nothing to build from. What the design does, said plainly, is the praise.

Message: '…' sells the design; describe it.

Looks for: cleanly, nicely, naturally, powerful, robust.

### ClauseCite (suggestion)

The statement's style: a clause is cited by its number alone, so the citation never outgrows the sentence it sits in.

Message: Cite a clause by its bare number in parentheses, as '(46)', not '…'.

Looks for: a pattern; see the rule.

### EmDash (suggestion)

An em dash lets two thoughts share a sentence without saying how they relate. A full stop or a comma makes the writer say it.

Message: An em dash joins two thoughts; give each its own sentence, or use a comma.

Looks for: —,  -- .

### Filler (suggestion)

Williams's concision lesson and Microsoft's 'be brief': a word that can leave without changing the meaning should leave.

Message: '…' adds nothing; cut it.

Looks for: simply, just, really, very, basically, actually, essentially, in fact, quite.

### Headings (suggestion)

Sentence case, as Google and Microsoft both set it, so a heading reads as a sentence and a proper noun stands out. Binds chapters only.

Message: Headings use sentence case: '…'.

### Metaphors (suggestion)

A metaphor used as justification replaces the reason a thing exists with a picture of it. The reason is what a builder needs.

Message: '…' is a metaphor standing in for a reason; give the reason, or use the plain word.

Looks for: source of truth, single pane of glass, north star, blessed path, pit of success, paved road, golden path, under the hood.

### Nominalization (suggestion)

Williams's nominalization test: when the action is a noun ('the formation of a candidate'), the subject is an abstraction and the verb is empty. Turn it back into a verb ('sluice forms a candidate').

Message: '…' hides the action in a noun; make it the verb.

Looks for: a pattern; see the rule.

### Passive (suggestion)

Williams: the passive hides the character, and a design book is about who does what. Allowed when the actor is unknown or does not matter, which is why this is a suggestion.

Message: '…' is passive; name the actor as the subject.

Looks for: a pattern; see the rule.

### SentenceLength (suggestion)

A long sentence is allowed when its subject and verb are its character and action; most long sentences are not. The limit is a prompt to look, not a ban.

Message: Sentences over 35 words are hard to follow; split it.

### ThereIs (suggestion)

Williams: a clear sentence has a character as its subject. 'There is' and 'there are' put a dummy in the subject's seat. Microsoft names them as weak writing to revise.

Message: '…' opens the sentence with no subject; name who does what.

Looks for: a pattern; see the rule.

### ThroatClearing (suggestion)

A phrase that precedes the point delays it. Microsoft's first tip and Williams's emphasis lesson agree: lead with what matters and end on it.

Message: '…' clears the throat; start with the point.

Looks for: of course, obviously, clearly, as mentioned, as noted, as stated, as described, needless to say, it goes without saying, in other words.

### Weasel (suggestion)

Taken from write-good's Weasel list, trimmed of words a design uses precisely. A weasel word makes a claim without committing to it; a chapter commits.

Message: '…' weakens the claim; say how much, or drop it.

Looks for: completely, exceedingly, extremely, huge, interestingly, largely, mostly, remarkably, substantially, surprisingly, tiny, usually, vast.
